nameStory: Small Spikerush gets its name from its diminutive size and the tiny spike-like flower cluster at the tip of each stem. The 'spike' isn't sharp like a thorn, but refers to the compact arrangement of minute flowers bunched together in what botanists call a spikelet. At barely taller than your thumb, this little plant lives up to its 'small' moniker!
description: Small Spikerush is a tiny perennial grass-like plant that forms small tufts in salty marshes and mudflats. Growing no taller than 4 inches, it produces clusters of thin, spongy green stems that feel soft and compressible when you gently squeeze them. Each stem is topped with a small oval flower spike that's barely bigger than a peppercorn. Despite its small stature, this hardy little plant thrives in the challenging conditions where salt water meets land.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms small tufts of thin, grass-like stems that grow from underground tubers, creating modest clumps in muddy areas

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Spongy, compressible stems that feel soft when gently squeezed, never more than 4 inches tall and bright green in color

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny oval-shaped spikelet at the tip of each stem, only 2-3 millimeters long and packed with several minute flowers

idTips.label: Underground Parts
idTips.description: Distinctive J-shaped or horseshoe-shaped tubers underground that can be carefully exposed for positive identification

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Entire plant feels soft and yielding, unlike the stiff, sharp edges of true grasses

habitat: Small Spikerush thrives in brackish and saltwater environments along New England's coast, particularly in salt marshes, tidal mudflats, and the edges of salt ponds. Look for it in areas that flood regularly with salt water, often growing alongside other salt-tolerant plants like glasswort and salt marsh asters. It prefers muddy, waterlogged soils that would be too salty for most other plants.

seasonality.spring: New green stems begin emerging from underground tubers as temperatures warm, forming fresh tufts in the muddy marsh substrate.
seasonality.summer: Peak growing season with fully developed spongy stems topped by tiny oval flower spikes, easily spotted in salt marsh communities.
seasonality.fall: Stems may begin to yellow and die back, though the plant remains identifiable by its distinctive tuft growth pattern.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground portions die back completely, leaving only the characteristic J-shaped tubers buried in the mud until spring.

funFact: Small Spikerush is popular in the aquarium trade under the name 'hairgrass' and can actually grow completely underwater, making it one of the few plants equally at home submerged in a fish tank or rooted in a salty marsh!
confusionNotes: Small Spikerush can be confused with other tiny grass-like plants in salt marshes, but the key is the spongy, compressible stems that feel soft when squeezed - true grasses have stiff, rigid stems with sharp edges that can actually cut your fingers.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'hairgrass' in aquarium circles, Small Spikerush isn't actually a grass at all - it belongs to the sedge family, which explains why its stems are soft and round rather than flat and sharp-edged like true grasses.
compareHints: Among New England's many spikerush species, Small Spikerush is distinguished by its extremely short stature (under 4 inches) and preference for salty habitats. Most other spikerushes like Common Spikerush grow much taller and prefer freshwater wetlands, while Small Spikerush's distinctive J-shaped underground tubers are unique among the genus.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the many spikerush species in New England, blunt spikerush stands out for its soft, spongy stems and distinctly rounded spikelets.
Needle Spikerush is the most delicate of all New England spikerushes, with stems so thin they make other species look chunky by comparison.
Unlike other spikerushes that grow in shallow water or wet soil, Robbins' Spikerush is the deep-water specialist of the genus, growing fully submerged in 1-4 feet of water.

Among the many spikerush species in New England, Black-fruited Spikerush is most easily distinguished by its dark seeds - Common Spikerush has pale tan seeds, while Needle Spikerush is much more delicate with thread-like stems.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Yellow Spikerush stands out for its pale, yellowish coloring and smaller stature compared to Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.
Among New England spikerushes, common spikerush is distinguished by its robust, colony-forming habit and relatively large flower spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Matted Spikerush is unique for its low, mat-forming growth habit - all its relatives grow upright.
Among its many spikerush relatives in New England, ovate spikerush stands out with its distinctly oval or egg-shaped flower spikes - most other spikerushes have more cylindrical or pointed spikes.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Slender Spikerush stands out for its particularly thin stems and small, oval flower spikes.
Among New England's spikerushes, Wright's is distinguished by its small size and the distinctive pyramid-shaped tubercle on its seeds.
Among the many New England spikerushes, Horsetail Spikerush is unique for its hollow, jointed stems - most other spikerushes have solid stems without visible segments.
Among the many spikerush species in New England, squarestem spikerush is the only one with distinctly four-angled stems - all the others have round or slightly flattened stems.

Few-flower Spikerush stands out from its many spikerush relatives primarily by its sparse flower count - most other New England spikerushes like Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush have dense, crowded spikelets with dozens of flowers.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Long-tubercled Spikerush stands out for its exceptionally large tubercle - up to 2.
Beaked spikerush differs from its many spikerush relatives primarily in its habitat preferences and the distinctive beaked tubercle on its seeds.
Among New England's spikerushes, Slender Spikerush has the thinnest stems - much thinner than Common Spikerush or Blunt Spikerush.

Among the spikerushes, Bald Spikerush stands out for its particularly wide, oval flower spikes with a reddish tint, unlike the narrow spikes of Needle Spikerush or the larger, brown spikes of Common Spikerush.

Unlike Common Spikerush which has smooth, round stems, or Needle Spikerush which forms dense mats of hair-thin stems, Threerib Spikerush is the only species in the genus with distinctly three-ribbed stems.
Among New England's many spikerushes, Creeping Spikerush is unique for its mat-forming, spreading growth pattern via underground runners.
